blocks.text: Iron mattered not because it suddenly replaced bronze on one day, but because its production, working and reproduction gradually became more reliable. More widely available ores opened possibilities, while charcoal, skilled workers and technique remained essential. Materials changed conditions without automatically creating institutions.

Assyria illustrates how intensive military organization could expand political scale. Expansion required continuing resource mobilization and increased pressures on government, transport and control. The reach of conquest and the capacity for lasting coordination are not the same measure.

blocks.caption: Zhou China · Context illustration; historical interpretation is in the text.

blocks.text: Persia offers a view of how a large empire could manage internal differences. Sustaining order across extensive territories did not necessarily require making every locality identical. Regions and groups needed connections that could continue to function.

The Zhou world of regional rulers, ritual and layered authority offered another arrangement. Comparing these societies is not a ranking of early empires. It reveals different combinations of materials, military organization and institutions, along with the costs each combination carried.
